title: Problems: the unit circle and waves

items.prose: A water wheel has radius 2.4 m, and its hub is 3 m above the river. A paddle tip T starts level with the hub, on the right. The wheel turns anticlockwise as you look at it.

parts.question: The tip travels 5.4 m along its circle. Through what angle has the wheel turned, in radians? Give a decimal.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Use $s = r\theta$ with the arc and the radius.

byKey.times: You multiplied the arc by the radius. Arc length is $s = r\theta$, so divide: $\theta = \tfrac{5.4}{2.4}$.
byKey.flipped: You divided the radius by the arc. The angle is arc over radius: $\tfrac{5.4}{2.4} = 2.25$.
byKey.turns: That is the fraction of a full turn, $\tfrac{5.4}{2\pi \times 2.4}$. In radians the angle is $\tfrac{s}{r} = 2.25$.

explain.text: Arc length is $s = r\theta$ with $\theta$ in radians. So $\theta = \tfrac{s}{r} = \tfrac{5.4}{2.4} = 2.25$. That lies between a quarter turn, $\tfrac{\pi}{2} \approx 1.57$, and a half turn, $\pi \approx 3.14$.

parts.question: Using 2.25 radians, what angle has the wheel turned in degrees? Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

feedback.generic: Not quite. A half turn is both $\pi$ radians and $180^\circ$.

byKey.wrong-way: You multiplied by $\tfrac{\pi}{180}$, which turns degrees into radians. To go back, multiply by $\tfrac{180}{\pi}$.
byKey.no-pi: You multiplied by 180 and left out the $\pi$. One radian is $\tfrac{180}{\pi} \approx 57.3^\circ$, so the answer is $2.25 \times 57.3$.

explain.text: A half turn is both $\pi$ radians and $180^\circ$, so one radian is $\tfrac{180}{\pi} \approx 57.3^\circ$. Then $2.25 \times \tfrac{180}{\pi} \approx 128.9^\circ$. The tip has passed the top of the wheel.

parts.question: With the wheel turned $128.9^\circ$, how high above the river is the tip? Give your answer in metres to 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. The tip is $2.4\sin\theta$ above the hub, and the hub is 3 m up.

byKey.radian-mode: That is $\sin 128.9$ worked out in radians. The angle is in degrees, so set the calculator to degrees: $\sin 128.9^\circ \approx 0.778$.
byKey.degree-mode: That is $\sin 2.25^\circ$: the radian angle typed in degree mode. Use $\sin 128.9^\circ$, or $\sin 2.25$ in radian mode.
byKey.cos: You used the cosine, the across-distance. The height above the hub is $2.4\sin\theta$.
byKey.no-hub: That is the height above the hub. Add the hub’s 3 m to get the height above the river.

explain.text: On a circle of radius 2.4, the tip is $2.4\sin\theta$ above the hub, the unit circle’s height scaled by 2.4. $\sin 128.9^\circ \approx 0.778$ is positive, because the tip is above the hub. So the height is $3 + 2.4 \times 0.778 \approx 4.87$ m.

parts.question: The wheel has turned $128.9^\circ$ and the tip is about 4.87 m above the river. Earlier in the same turn, the tip was at exactly this height on the other side of the top. At what angle, in degrees, was that? Give your answer to 1 decimal place.

feedback.correct: $180^\circ - 128.9^\circ = 51.1^\circ$, the mirror image in the vertical axis.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Points at the same height are mirror images in the vertical axis through the hub.

byKey.cos-mirror: That is $360^\circ - 128.9^\circ$, the mirror in the horizontal axis, which keeps the cosine. For the same height use $180^\circ - 128.9^\circ$.
byKey.half-turn: Half a turn on puts the tip below the hub, with the opposite height. The mirror in the vertical axis is $180^\circ - 128.9^\circ$.
byKey.minus-90: You took $90^\circ$ off. The two angles sit equally far either side of $90^\circ$: $90 - 38.9 = 51.1$.

explain.text: Points at the same height are mirror images in the vertical axis through the hub. The mirror of $\theta$ is $180^\circ - \theta$, and $\sin(180^\circ - \theta) = \sin\theta$. So the tip was at this height at $180^\circ - 128.9^\circ = 51.1^\circ$.

parts.question: Using $51.1^\circ$, how far along its circle had the tip travelled from the start at that moment? Give your answer in metres to 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Turn the angle into radians, then use $s = r\theta$.

byKey.degrees: You used $s = r\theta$ with $\theta$ in degrees. Turn $51.1^\circ$ into radians first: about 0.892.
byKey.divided: You divided the angle by the radius. Arc length multiplies: $s = r\theta$, with $\theta$ in radians.
byKey.between: That is the arc between the two moments, $5.4 - 2.14$. The question asks for the arc from the start: 2.14 m.

explain.text: Turn the angle into radians first: $51.1 \times \tfrac{\pi}{180} \approx 0.892$. Then $s = r\theta = 2.4 \times 0.892 \approx 2.14$ m. Check: the top is $2.4 \times \tfrac{\pi}{2} \approx 3.77$ m round, and 2.14 m and 5.4 m sit 1.63 m either side of it.

items.prose: Two buoys bob up and down on the same swell. The first buoy’s height above the harbour floor is $h = 6 + 0.8\sin\left(\tfrac{\pi t}{5}\right)$ metres. Here $t$ is in seconds after a timer starts, and the angle is in radians.

parts.question: What is the period of the first buoy’s motion, in seconds? Give a whole number.

feedback.generic: Not quite. One wave is drawn while the angle runs from 0 to $2\pi$.

byKey.read-five: The 5 divides $\pi t$, but the period is $2\pi \div \tfrac{\pi}{5}$. The angle needs $2\pi$, not $\pi$, for one full wave.
byKey.b-itself: That is $b = \tfrac{\pi}{5}$ itself. The period is $\tfrac{2\pi}{b} = 10$.
byKey.times: You multiplied $2\pi$ by $b$. The period divides: $\tfrac{2\pi}{\pi/5} = 10$.

explain.text: One wave is drawn while the angle $\tfrac{\pi t}{5}$ runs from 0 to $2\pi$. That happens while $t$ runs from 0 to 10. So the period is $2\pi \div \tfrac{\pi}{5} = 10$ seconds.

parts.question: The wave starts at its middle line, rising, at $t = 0$. Using the period of 10 seconds, when does the first buoy first reach its highest point? Give your answer in seconds as a decimal.

feedback.correct: A peak comes a quarter of a period after the rising start: $\tfrac{10}{4} = 2.5$ s.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Sine peaks a quarter of the way through each wave.

byKey.angle: That is $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$, the angle at the peak. Solve $\tfrac{\pi t}{5} = \tfrac{\pi}{2}$ for $t$: $t = 2.5$.
byKey.half: At half a period the buoy is back at its middle line, falling. The peak comes a quarter of the way through: 2.5 s.
byKey.trough: At three quarters of a period the buoy is at its lowest. The peak comes a quarter of the way through: 2.5 s.

explain.text: Sine peaks when its angle is $\tfrac{\pi}{2}$, a quarter of a turn. Here $\tfrac{\pi t}{5} = \tfrac{\pi}{2}$ gives $t = 2.5$, a quarter of the 10-second period. At $t = 5$ the buoy is back at its middle line, falling.

parts.question: The second buoy follows $h = 6 + 0.8\sin\left(\tfrac{\pi (t - 3)}{5}\right)$, the same wave 3 seconds later. Using the first buoy’s peak at 2.5 s, when does the second buoy first reach its highest point? Give your answer in seconds as a decimal.

feedback.correct: A shift of 3 to the right moves every peak 3 s later: $2.5 + 3 = 5.5$ s.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which way does $t - 3$ slide the wave?

byKey.early: You moved the peak 3 s earlier. Writing $t - 3$ for $t$ slides the wave to the right, so everything happens 3 s later.
byKey.lag: That is the lag itself. Add it to the first buoy’s peak time: $2.5 + 3 = 5.5$ s.

explain.text: Writing $t - 3$ in place of $t$ slides the graph 3 to the right, so every point happens 3 seconds later. The first peak moves from 2.5 s to 5.5 s. Check: at $t = 5.5$ the angle is $\tfrac{\pi \times 2.5}{5} = \tfrac{\pi}{2}$.

parts.question: At $t = 5.5$ s the second buoy is at its peak, 6.8 m. How far below it is the first buoy at that moment? Give your answer in metres to 2 decimal places.

feedback.correct: The first buoy is at $6 + 0.8\sin(1.1\pi) \approx 6 - 0.247 = 5.753$ m, so it is $6.8 - 5.753 \approx 1.05$ m lower.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find the first buoy’s height at $t = 5.5$, with the angle in radians.

byKey.height: That is the first buoy’s height. The question asks for the gap: $6.8 - 5.75 \approx 1.05$ m.
byKey.degree-mode: That uses $\sin(1.1\pi)$ in degree mode. The angle $1.1\pi$ is in radians, where its sine is about $-0.309$.
byKey.full-swing: That is the full swing from peak to trough. The first buoy is not at its trough at 5.5 s.

explain.text: At $t = 5.5$ the first buoy’s angle is $\tfrac{5.5\pi}{5} = 1.1\pi$, just past a half turn, where sine is negative. So its height is $6 + 0.8\sin(1.1\pi) \approx 6 - 0.247 = 5.753$ m. The gap is $6.8 - 5.753 \approx 1.05$ m.

items.prose: An observation wheel has a diameter of 50 m, and its hub is 28 m above the ground. It turns once every 20 minutes, and a rider boards at the lowest point at $t = 0$. The rider’s height in metres is $h = a\sin\big(b(t - c)\big) + d$, with $t$ in minutes and the angle in radians.

parts.question: What is the amplitude $a$, in metres? Give a whole number.

feedback.correct: The rider swings one radius either side of the hub, so $a = 25$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. How far above and below the hub does the rider go?

byKey.diameter: That is the whole swing from bottom to top. The amplitude is the swing either side of the hub: half of 50.
byKey.top: That is the highest point, $28 + 25$. The amplitude is the distance from the middle line to the top: 25.
byKey.hub: That is the middle line $d$, the hub’s height. The amplitude is the radius, 25.

explain.text: The rider swings one radius above and one radius below the hub. The radius is half of 50 m, so $a = 25$. The height runs from $28 - 25 = 3$ m to $28 + 25 = 53$ m.

parts.question: Using one turn every 20 minutes, what is $b$? Give an exact multiple of $\pi$.

feedback.correct: $b = \tfrac{2\pi}{20} = \tfrac{\pi}{10}$, so the angle grows by a full turn every 20 minutes.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The period of $\sin(bt)$ is $\tfrac{2\pi}{b}$.

byKey.period: That is the period. The period is $\tfrac{2\pi}{b}$, so $b = \tfrac{2\pi}{20}$.
byKey.half: That uses $\pi$ for a full turn. A full turn is $2\pi$, so $b = \tfrac{2\pi}{20} = \tfrac{\pi}{10}$.
byKey.flipped: You turned the fraction upside down. From $\tfrac{2\pi}{b} = 20$, $b = \tfrac{2\pi}{20}$.

explain.text: The period of $\sin(bt)$ is $\tfrac{2\pi}{b}$, and here the period is 20 minutes. So $\tfrac{2\pi}{b} = 20$, which gives $b = \tfrac{2\pi}{20} = \tfrac{\pi}{10}$. That is about 0.314 radians each minute.

parts.question: The rider boards at the bottom. A quarter of a turn later, the model crosses its middle line going up. Using the period of 20 minutes, what is the shift $c$, in minutes? Give a whole number.

feedback.correct: A quarter of 20 minutes is 5, so $c = 5$ and $h = 25\sin\big(\tfrac{\pi}{10}(t - 5)\big) + 28$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Find when the rider reaches hub height on the way up.

byKey.boarding: At $t = 0$ the rider is at the bottom, not at the middle line. The rising crossing comes a quarter turn later.
byKey.top: At 10 minutes the rider is at the top. The shift is the time of the rising crossing of the middle line.
byKey.falling: At 15 minutes the rider crosses the middle line going down. The shift needs the upward crossing.

explain.text: In $a\sin\big(b(t - c)\big) + d$, the shift $c$ is a time when $h$ crosses the middle line going up. The rider reaches hub height a quarter of a turn after boarding, at $\tfrac{20}{4} = 5$ minutes. Check: at $t = 0$ the angle is $-\tfrac{\pi}{2}$, so $h = 28 - 25 = 3$ m, the bottom.

parts.question: Using $h = 25\sin\big(\tfrac{\pi}{10}(t - 5)\big) + 28$, how high is the rider 8 minutes after boarding? Give your answer in metres to 2 decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Work out the bracket $t - 5$ first, and keep the angle in radians.

byKey.degree-mode: That works out $\sin(0.3\pi)$ in degree mode. The angle is in radians, so $\sin(0.3\pi) \approx 0.809$.
byKey.no-shift: That uses $\tfrac{\pi}{10} \times 8$ and leaves out the shift. The bracket is $t - 5 = 3$, so the angle is $0.3\pi$.

explain.text: At $t = 8$ the bracket is $8 - 5 = 3$, so the angle is $0.3\pi$ radians. Then $\sin(0.3\pi) \approx 0.809$, and $h \approx 25 \times 0.809 + 28 = 48.23$ m. That is 2 minutes before the top at $t = 10$, so the rider is close to the 53 m peak.

parts.question: The rider is at the top at $t = 10$. At what other time in the first turn is the rider at the same height as at $t = 8$? Give a whole number of minutes.

feedback.correct: The graph is symmetric about its peak at $t = 10$, so 2 minutes after the top matches 2 minutes before: $t = 12$.
feedback.generic: Not quite. The height graph is symmetric about its peak.

byKey.no-shift: That solves $t - 5 = 7$ but stops there. Add the 5 back: $t = 12$.
byKey.half-period: Half a turn later the rider is on the opposite side, near the bottom. The matching time is the mirror about the top at $t = 10$.
byKey.mirror-start: That mirrors $t = 8$ about $t = 5$, where the rider is at hub height. Heights match either side of the top, $t = 10$.

explain.text: Sine takes the same value at the angles $\theta$ and $\pi - \theta$, mirror images on the unit circle. Here $\pi - 0.3\pi = 0.7\pi$, so $\tfrac{\pi}{10}(t - 5) = 0.7\pi$ and $t - 5 = 7$, giving $t = 12$. That is 2 minutes after the top, as 8 is 2 minutes before it.
